reference.source: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
clinicalPearls: Faecal impaction is a large, firm, immovable mass of stool in the rectum or colon that cannot be evacuated spontaneously, most often complicating chronic constipation
Overflow (spurious) diarrhoea and faecal soiling around an impacted mass are classic and are easily misdiagnosed as simple diarrhoea, leading to inappropriate treatment
It is especially common in older, immobile, cognitively impaired, or institutionalised patients and in those on constipating drugs such as opioids and anticholinergics
Digital rectal examination revealing a rectum loaded with hard stool is the key bedside diagnostic step; a high impaction may leave an empty rectum despite proximal loading
Plain abdominal radiography helps assess the extent of colonic loading and exclude obstruction or perforation
Management combines rectal disimpaction (softening enemas or suppositories, and gentle manual disimpaction when needed) followed by oral laxatives and a maintenance bowel regimen
Complications include stercoral ulceration, colonic perforation, urinary retention, and, rarely, large-bowel obstruction
Prevention through adequate fibre, hydration, mobility, laxatives with opioids, and toileting routines is central to avoiding recurrence
reference.pathophysiology: Faecal impaction develops when colonic transit and rectal evacuation are sufficiently impaired that stool dehydrates and hardens into an immovable mass. Prolonged colonic residence allows excessive water reabsorption, producing progressively firmer stool. Reduced rectal sensation, impaired rectal contractility, weakened pelvic-floor and abdominal effort, and blunted defecatory reflexes, as occur with ageing, neurological disease, immobility, and constipating medications, prevent effective expulsion. The retained mass distends the rectum, and chronic distension further diminishes rectal sensation and the urge to defecate, perpetuating retention. Liquid stool from above may track around the mass, producing overflow incontinence, while sustained pressure on the rectal mucosa can cause stercoral ulceration and, at worst, ischaemic necrosis and perforation.
additionalDifferentials: Mechanical large-bowel obstruction from stricture or tumour
Infective or inflammatory diarrhoea (when overflow is mistaken for true diarrhoea)
Hirschsprung disease or other neuromuscular colonic disorder in younger patients
Pelvic mass causing extrinsic rectal compression
additionalInvestigations: Digital rectal examination to confirm rectal loading and assess stool consistency
Plain abdominal radiograph to gauge faecal loading and exclude obstruction or free air
Full blood count, electrolytes, calcium, and thyroid function to identify contributory metabolic causes
CT of the abdomen and pelvis where obstruction, perforation, or an underlying mass is suspected
Colonoscopy or contrast enema after resolution if an obstructing lesion is possible
Review of medication and mobility as contributory factors
redFlags: Abdominal distension with pain, guarding, or peritonism suggesting perforation
Rectal bleeding raising concern for stercoral ulceration or an underlying tumour
Features of large-bowel obstruction such as vomiting and absolute constipation
Systemic sepsis or signs of ischaemia
Acute urinary retention from pelvic pressure
reference.prognosis: Uncomplicated faecal impaction usually resolves with disimpaction and a maintenance bowel regimen, but it frequently recurs unless underlying causes are corrected; complicated impaction with stercoral ulceration or perforation carries significant morbidity and mortality, particularly in frail older patients.
pitfalls: Mistaking overflow soiling for infective diarrhoea and prescribing antidiarrhoeal agents
Missing a high impaction because the rectum is empty on examination
Overlooking an obstructing tumour or stricture as the underlying cause
Failing to establish a maintenance regimen, leading to recurrence
Forceful disimpaction risking mucosal injury, bleeding, or perforation
references: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
NICE guidance on the management of constipation and faecal impaction
Standard geriatric and coloproctology reference texts on chronic constipation
management: Rectal disimpaction with softening or osmotic enemas, glycerol or bisacodyl suppositories, and gentle manual disimpaction of a low hard mass
Oral osmotic laxatives such as macrogol to clear proximal colonic loading and a high impaction
Establishment of a maintenance bowel regimen with regular laxatives, adequate fluid intake and dietary fibre
Review and rationalisation of constipating drugs such as opioids and anticholinergics, with co-prescription of laxatives alongside opioids
Optimisation of mobility and toileting, and correction of contributory metabolic causes such as hypothyroidism and hypercalcaemia
Monitoring for complications including overflow incontinence, stercoral ulceration, obstruction and perforation
Colonoscopy or imaging after resolution if an obstructing lesion is suspected, with surgical referral for perforation or obstruction
